segments.t: At the elevator doors of ASK, former managing partner Mathias Barneville prepares to leave the agency for good. Holding his box of personal belongings, he is confronted by Andrea, who firmly asks him to return his office keys. Let's listen to their farewell conversation in French first.
Mathias, attends une seconde s'il te plaît.
Oui Andréa? Qu'est-ce qu'il y a?
Tu dois nous rendre tes clés d'agence.
Vous me traitez comme un voleur maintenant?
Noémie a déjà rendu les siennes ce matin.
J'ai dirigé cette agence pendant trente ans!
Nous voulons simplement protéger nos nouveaux contrats.
Vous avez peur de ma concurrence future?
Nous voulons éviter de changer les serrures.
Prends ces clés, je n'en veux plus.
Merci Mathias, bonne chance pour tes projets.
Au revoir. Vraiment, je n'en reviens pas.
Une nouvelle histoire commence pour nous tous.
Bonne chance avec vos nouveaux problèmes quotidiens!
Let's examine the conversation line by line and explore the French expressions.
Mathias, attends une seconde s'il te plaît.
'Mathias, wait a second please.' Andrea stops Mathias before he reaches the lift. The reflexive pronoun sits right in front of the verb for 'wait', turning the action back onto the subject.
Oui Andréa? Qu'est-ce qu'il y a?
'Yes Andrea? What is the matter?' Mathias wonders what further request remains. Notice how the short vowel drops before a vowel sound around 'is there', making the phrase flow smoothly as one unit.
Tu dois nous rendre tes clés d'agence.
'You must give back your agency keys.' Andrea requests the surrender of his keys. Notice how 'must' leads directly into the noun meaning 'keys'.
Vous me traitez comme un voleur maintenant?
'Are you treating me like a thief now?' Mathias feels insulted by the demand. Mathias uses the polite 'you' form alongside 'treat' to keep a respectful professional tone.
Noémie a déjà rendu les siennes ce matin.
'Noemie already gave back hers this morning.' Andrea mentions Noemie's compliance. The verb meaning 'has' pairs naturally with the noun for 'morning' in everyday conversation.
J'ai dirigé cette agence pendant trente ans!
'I ran this agency for thirty years!' Mathias recalls his long-standing authority. This conversational past tense combines a helper verb with the past participle for 'managed'.
Nous voulons simplement protéger nos nouveaux contrats.
'We simply want to protect our new contracts.' Andrea defends client confidentiality. The descriptive adjective for 'new' agrees in gender and number with its noun.
Vous avez peur de ma concurrence future?
'Are you afraid of my future competition?' Mathias suspects fear of his new firm. The verb meaning 'have' pairs naturally with the noun for 'fear' in everyday conversation.
Nous voulons éviter de changer les serrures.
'We want to avoid changing the locks.' Andrea provides a pragmatic financial reason. Notice how 'want' leads directly into the noun meaning 'locks'.
Prends ces clés, je n'en veux plus.
'Take these keys, I do not want them anymore.' Mathias gives in with irritation. The verb meaning 'take' pairs naturally with the noun for 'keys' in everyday conversation.
Merci Mathias, bonne chance pour tes projets.
'Thank you Mathias, good luck with your projects.' Andrea offers civil farewell wishes. The key noun here means 'thank you', anchored by its matching French article.
Au revoir. Vraiment, je n'en reviens pas.
'Goodbye. Seriously, I cannot believe it.' Mathias shakes his head in disbelief. The verb meaning 'return' pairs naturally with the noun for 'goodbye' in everyday conversation.
Une nouvelle histoire commence pour nous tous.
'A new story begins for all of us.' Andrea looks forward to leading the agency. The adjective meaning 'new' takes its feminine form here to match the noun it describes.
Bonne chance avec vos nouveaux problèmes quotidiens!

'Good luck with your new daily problems!' Mathias delivers a sardonic parting remark. Mathias uses the polite 'you' form alongside 'luck' to keep a respectful professional tone. Now let's listen to the complete discussion once more to reinforce the vocabulary.

Mathias hands over his keys and steps into the closing elevator, bringing thirty years at ASK to an end. When you watch the episode, listen out for the expressions meaning 'wait' and 'second'. You'll catch them now. See you next time.
